newsitem.title: BELGIUM: U.S.-French row over command still seen continuing.
newsitem.headline: U.S.-French row over command still seen continuing.

text.p: A row between France and the United States over who should run NATO's southern command is unlikely to go away despite a more conciliatory tone from Paris, alliance sources said on Friday.

Speaking as chiefs of defence staff from the 16-nation North Atlantic Treaty Organisation met to discuss how to create a leaner, more efficient command structure, the sources said they expected alliance leaders would still have to solve the dispute.
"It can only be sorted out at the highest political levels. But we will find a solution," one NATO source said.

At issue is France's insistence that the commander of AFSOUTH, NATO's southern command in Naples, must be a European, reflecting the continent's desire to develop a European security identity within the alliance.
France has said it will consider stepping back from its commitment to rejoin NATO's military command if it is not satisfied with NATO's Europeanisation.
The United States, however, has ruled out giving up the AFSOUTH command, which is responsible for the U.S. Sixth Fleet and is integral to Washington's Middle East policy.
France on Thursday appeared to tone down its demand, when Defence Minister Charles Millon told NATO parliamentarians in Versailles he believed thw issue could be solved.
"You know there is a discussion on this point with our American friends who have raised a number of questions. I believe they can be answered," he said.
But NATO sources said on Friday that France was still firmly committed to the idea of a European at AFSOUTH.
"I wouldn't over-interpret this," one said. "France still sees (a European AFSOUTH) as a fundamental requirement."
The NATO defence chiefs of staff were meeting to discuss how to change the shape of NATO to reflect the end of the Cold War.
Most countries are seeking to cut back the number of NATO headquarters. There are now 65, but planners would like to trim the number by about half.
A key element of the planning is to cut Europe's three regional commands -- in Britain, the Netherlands and Italy -- to just two.
The British command would go, leaving a simple northern and southern command structure. France wants both posts to be held by Europeans.
Military sources have said the defence chiefs would not be able to recommend a new command structure to their political masters because of the U.S.-French row.
One source said he expected the issue would go all the way to the next summit of NATO leaders, expected to be held next summer.
